clue.text: Stone found in bad pastry – not part of standard run

blocks.note: food gone bad has gone off
a pie is a pastry dish; it holds the stone
st = stone, the unit of weight

explanation.surface: A diner bites on a stone baked into a bad pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash splits the clue: everything before it is wordplay, and 'standard run' means a groomed ski run, not a jog or a print run.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-piste skiing happens away from the marked, groomed runs.

clue.text: Cool down number two distributor in trouble

blocks.note: to cool someone by wafting air at them
in the saying, trouble arrives when muck hits this and it sprays the mess everywhere

explanation.surface: An instruction to calm a deputy who is spreading trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number two' is a childish word for excrement, so the second definition is the saying 'when the shit hits the fan', dressed up politely.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan cools you down, and in the saying it is what scatters the mess when things go wrong.

clue.text: Father starts preaching about Tibet’s esoteric religions

indicators.note: take the start of each following word

blocks.note: the first letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A priest begins a sermon on the mystical faiths of Tibet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father' reads as a priest doing the preaching, but it is the definition: pater is Latin for father, and old-fashioned British slang for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Pater is Latin for father and a jokey old British word for one's dad.

clue.text: Makes purchases when inebriated? They’ll be so dirty

indicators.note: joins the two halves: shops, when oiled

explanation.surface: A drunk goes on a spending spree and ends up grubby.
explanation.walkthrough: Oiled is British slang for drunk. The question mark flags that the wordplay is read literally as someone who shops while oiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Shop-soiled goods have got grubby or worn from being on display in a shop.

clue.text: Native elements in Nazareth nicely hidden

indicators.note: the answer is made of parts of the next words
the answer is concealed in the words

explanation.surface: Local things are neatly concealed in Nazareth.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is split around its fodder, with 'elements in' before and 'hidden' after.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnic means belonging to a people by birth or origin, much as native does.

clue.text: I request silence during plot slip-up

blocks.note: to plot is to map, and a plot is a map

explanation.surface: Someone shushes the audience during a plot twist that goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Plot here is a map or chart, not a story line.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a small accident or blunder.

clue.text: Section of Bremen University that deals with consumer choice

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase for the thing, 'what deals with consumer choice'

indicators.note: the answer is a section of the next words

explanation.surface: A department of a German university studies consumer behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an economics faculty; the consumer is really a diner choosing from a menu.
explanation.definitionFit: A menu sets out the choices a customer can make.

clue.text: Figure first possessed by a kind of spark

explanation.surface: A figure is caught up in the first flash of inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: IST is 1ST with the digit read as the letter I, a standard trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: figure in its numerical sense, a single piece of counted data.

clue.text: It changes text to cure actor rambling

indicators.note: the letters wander out of order

explanation.surface: Some tool edits a script to stop an actor going off on tangents.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is everything between the definition and the indicator, 'to' included.
explanation.definitionFit: Autocorrect is the phone or computer feature that alters what you type.

clue.text: Combination hits in boxing results in very short count

blocks.note: a jab followed at once by a cross, two punches in quick succession
a count that stops at the second number

explanation.surface: A boxer's combination ends with the opponent down for barely a count.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxing surface makes 'count' look like the referee's count; it is just counting to two.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are literal: the boxing term for a two-punch combination, and the shortest count past one.

clue.text: Women’s group eager to host northern prince

blocks.note: a hearty appetite is an eager one

explanation.surface: A women's club is keen to welcome a royal from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen party is the British name for a bride's night out with her friends before the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen party is a gathering of women, usually the bride-to-be's friends.

clue.text: Arrogant British cut short broadcast

blocks.note: CUT with its end cut off

explanation.surface: An arrogant Briton's broadcast is taken off air early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut short' looks like a single instruction to trim British; in fact cut is itself the word that gets shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: Hubristic means showing hubris, excessive pride or arrogance.

clue.text: Leading composer slipped up, losing right to be covered

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it

blocks.note: a team that is up is leading
Gustav Holst, composer of The Planets
R = right; removed from ERRED to leave ERED

explanation.surface: A leading composer made a mistake and got a bad review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading composer' looks like one phrase for a famous musician, but 'Leading' works alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Upholstered furniture is covered with padding and fabric.

clue.text: Put forward idea for sports ground

blocks.note: to propose, as a salesman does
the field for football or cricket

explanation.surface: Someone proposes a scheme for a new stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a pitch is the playing field for football, rugby or cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: You pitch an idea to sell it, and a pitch is the ground games are played on.

clue.text: Spied broken wire – that’s disgraceful

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A spy is caught snooping on a cut wire, which is shameful.
explanation.walkthrough: Only part of the fodder is printed: wire must first become CABLE before the letters are mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Despicable means deserving contempt, disgraceful.

clue.text: Occasionally forgot duo’s name for this little character

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only some letters are used: every other one

blocks.note: F-R-O-D-O: the odd letters of forgot duo
Frodo names one of these creatures: the definition asks what kind of character he is

explanation.surface: Someone keeps forgetting the name of a double act's small sidekick.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate letters do not spell the answer; they spell FRODO, and the clue then asks what Frodo is the name of.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobbits are Tolkien's small folk, and Frodo Baggins is the best known.

clue.text: Benefit cuts for remote regions in the US

blocks.note: to dock pay is to cut it

explanation.surface: Welfare cuts hit the far-flung parts of America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Benefit cuts' reads as one phrase about welfare, and British readers know 'benefits' as state welfare payments.
explanation.definitionFit: The boondocks is American slang for remote backcountry.

clue.text: In drink, lieutenant is very loud singer

explanation.surface: A drunken officer turns out to be a very loud singer.
explanation.walkthrough: A belter is a singer who belts songs out at full volume.
explanation.definitionFit: To belt out a song is to sing it loudly, so a belter is a loud singer.

clue.text: Assistant abandoned waste outlet cleaner in Dublin, he’s a fool

definitions.note: the definition is 'fool', qualified as Irish usage by 'in Dublin'

blocks.note: loo paper cleans up at the loo
PA = personal assistant, taken out of LOO PAPER

explanation.surface: An Irish cleaner's helper walks off the job, and he is called a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Loo is British for toilet. 'Waste outlet cleaner' sounds like a drain unblocker, but it is the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: In Irish slang a looper is a crazy or foolish person.

clue.text: First nation warrior is a bit erratic sounding

indicators.note: the answer sounds like the phrase

blocks.note: patchy = erratic, uneven; 'a patchy' is the phrase said aloud

explanation.surface: A warrior of a native people behaves somewhat unpredictably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit erratic' has to be turned into 'a patchy' before it is said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apache are a Native American people, famed as warriors.

clue.text: Become keen on second opinion although it lacks weight

indicators.note: to lack something is to be without it

blocks.note: a take is an opinion, and two is the second
W = weight, the letter taken out

explanation.surface: Someone warms to a second opinion even though it carries little weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take two' is a second take; losing W leaves the phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To take to something is to start liking it.

clue.text: Musical composition incorporates core elements of Goethe and Auden

indicators.note: take the middle letters of each name

explanation.surface: A piece of music draws on the heart of Goethe's and Auden's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Goethe has an even number of letters, so its core is two letters; Auden's is three.
explanation.definitionFit: An étude is a short musical study, written to practise a technique.

clue.text: Doctor sat in cafe entrance

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it

explanation.surface: A doctor sits in a café doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: Entrance is the verb, stressed on the second syllable, not the doorway the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to hold them spellbound, to fascinate them.

clue.text: Musicians include individual piece in sacred text

explanation.surface: A band adds a solo to a setting of scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: A nonet is a group of nine players, or the piece written for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by group size: any ensemble of nine players is a nonet.

clue.text: Mass chubby priest cut

indicators.note: to cut something is to remove it

blocks.note: P = priest, the letter taken out

explanation.surface: A tubby priest cuts short the Mass.
explanation.walkthrough: Mass sits next to priest to suggest a church service; it is a lump, a shapeless mass.
explanation.definitionFit: A lump is a solid mass with no particular shape.

clue.text: Male friend in US picked up firm promotional material

indicators.note: heard, as a radio picks up a signal

blocks.note: bro, American slang for a brother or buddy

explanation.surface: An American buddy lands some advertising work for his company.
explanation.walkthrough: Firm looks like a company to go with the promotional material; it is the adjective, sure.
explanation.definitionFit: A brochure is a booklet advertising a product or service.

clue.text: Pop group, by covering single, gets millions

explanation.surface: A band covering someone else's single makes millions.
explanation.walkthrough: The music surface makes 'covering' and 'single' look like a cover version of a record. Boney M were a 1970s disco group.
explanation.definitionFit: Boney M were a disco group with hits such as Rivers of Babylon.

clue.text: Finally try tofu cream – it’s delicious

indicators.note: take the final letter of each word

explanation.surface: A diner finally tries tofu cream and declares it tasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' looks like it belongs to the surface's 'at last I tried it'; it applies to every word, not just one.
explanation.definitionFit: Yum is what you say when something tastes delicious.

clue.text: It makes sense to link supplement to drink …

definitions.note: 'it adds up' = it makes sense; the answer is the verb phrase

blocks.note: to supplement is to add to

explanation.surface: A health tip: taking a supplement with a drink is sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into the next clue, but this clue works alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: when a story adds up its figures tally, so it hangs together.

clue.text: … eventually it will provide extra income?

blocks.note: given enough time; in the end
hours worked beyond the normal day are paid on top of wages

explanation.surface: Continuing the last clue: the supplement will pay off in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, over time means eventually; as one word, it is the extra hours that earn extra pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: read as two words it means eventually; as one it is the paid extra hours.
